dataset.title: NASA Moon to Mars Architecture Definition Document — Revision C
dataset.note: Priority rankings and bins are NASA values. Detailed traceability below is included only where verified from NASA Revision C source material; no missing mapping is inferred.

technology_gaps.title: Lunar Dust-Tolerant Systems and Dust Mitigation
technology_gaps.description: Lunar dust is a concern for EVA, mobility, habitats, power and other surface assets. Long-life lunar systems require hardware and mitigation methods that remain operable in the abrasive, electrostatically charged dust environment.
technology_gaps.impact_if_unresolved: NASA states that systems may be damaged by dust particles and may not perform at expected reliability or duration.
technology_gaps.current_state: Apollo-era dust-tolerant approaches and terrestrial analog hardware exist, but applicability to long-duration lunar operations requires further development and environmental validation.
technology_gaps.performance_target: Systems able to operate efficiently for expected mission durations while preventing extreme wear and limiting dust accumulation or transfer into habitable spaces.

technology_gaps.title: Extreme Environment Avionics
technology_gaps.description: Exploration avionics must tolerate extreme temperature, radiation, dust and vacuum conditions over mission durations where current state-of-the-art systems are insufficient.
technology_gaps.impact_if_unresolved: NASA identifies consequences including additional shielding or insulation, more active thermal control, increased failures and maintenance, reduced high-performance processing capability, and reduced autonomy.
technology_gaps.current_state: Existing spacecraft subsystems cover limited thermal and radiation environments; only a limited number of vacuum-tolerant systems exist for the full exploration envelope.
technology_gaps.performance_target: Enable avionics to tolerate and survive the extreme environments expected on the Moon and Mars, with increased reliability and lower maintenance burden.

technology_gaps.title: Systems to Survive and Operate through Extended Periods of Lunar Shadow
technology_gaps.description: Long-duration lunar assets need integrated power, thermal-management and actuation technologies that can survive the Moon's extreme shadowed environment.
technology_gaps.impact_if_unresolved: NASA states that failure to close this gap can shorten the operating life of surface assets and may prevent their reuse after shadowed periods.
technology_gaps.current_state: Small spacecraft have survived lunar shadow with subsystem damage and degraded capability; NASA reports no human-scale state of the art for repeated extended shadow operation.
technology_gaps.performance_target: Survive continuous lunar shadow for 350 hours or more, several times per year, for 10 years.

technology_gaps.title: Cryogenic Fluid Transfer
technology_gaps.description: NASA ranks cryogenic fluid transfer fourth in Revision C. The capability supports low-loss transfer of cryogenic fluids for exploration transportation and refueling applications.
technology_gaps.impact_if_unresolved: Detailed Revision C traceability is intentionally not reproduced in this prototype until its current mapping is ingested from the official table.

technology_gaps.title: High-bandwidth, High-reliability Surface-to-Surface Communications
technology_gaps.description: Moon and Mars surface systems need secure, scalable and interoperable communications for crew, robotics, habitats, infrastructure and mobility assets across exploration distances.
technology_gaps.impact_if_unresolved: NASA states that the architecture would lack reliable, high-bandwidth lunar and Martian surface communications able to scale across multiple users, providers and assets.
technology_gaps.current_state: Heritage UHF and ISS Wi-Fi demonstrate pieces of the capability but do not provide the required lunar surface mission-critical network.
technology_gaps.performance_target: For the Moon, NASA identifies scalable interoperable technologies supporting approximately 25–50 Mbps within 10 km for multiple users, including mission-critical voice, video, navigation and data.

technology_gaps.title: Mars Transportation Propulsion
technology_gaps.description: Human Mars missions require propulsion capable of transporting large human-class systems to Mars vicinity. NASA is evaluating nuclear, non-nuclear, high-thrust, low-thrust and hybrid options.
technology_gaps.impact_if_unresolved: NASA states that without gap closure the propulsion trade space may be constrained to only a few options, substantially increasing Mars mission cost or threatening viability.
technology_gaps.current_state: Chemical propulsion is mature, while aggregation of chemical propellant has not been demonstrated on orbit at the required scale; NTP and NEP remain low-TRL at human-exploration scale and SEP may require substantial scaling.
technology_gaps.performance_target: Enable crew and cargo transportation between Earth and Mars; detailed performance is driven by ongoing architecture definition tasks.
